# The Truth, the Whole Truth, and Nothing but the Map

Every map tells the truth. No map tells the whole truth. This paradox sits at the heart of cartography: a map can be scrupulously accurate at every point and still lead its reader badly astray. The problem is not lying—maps that simply falsify are a different beast. The problem is that accuracy is not the same as honesty, and honesty is not the same as completeness. A map is always a selection, a compression, an argument about what matters. Understanding how maps choose is essential to reading them well.

## The Tyranny of Scale

Consider the humble hiking map. A standard topographic trail map might render the world at a scale of 1:24,000, meaning one inch on paper equals 24,000 inches (about 2,000 feet) of terrain. That sounds impressively detailed, and it is—but scale is a promise and a limitation at once. At 1:24,000, a trail three feet wide cannot be drawn three feet wide on paper; it would be invisible.
